say.text: A well 50-year-old man has no peritonism. His erect film shows gas under the right dome, with haustral markings.
Free gas, or not? Make your call.

choices.label: Chilaiditi sign: colon lying beneath the diaphragm, not free gas
Free gas: it sits under the right dome, where free gas rises
Free gas, so the cause is a perforated ulcer and theatre
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Gas lying in the colon's own pattern, between liver and diaphragm, is a pseudo-pneumoperitoneum.
The real question is whether the gas is inside the bowel or outside it, not just where it sits.

choices.label: I can see it: skip the walk-through

say.text: That choice is not right.
Free gas does rise under the right dome, so the place looks right, but a place is not a diagnosis.
Ask whether this gas sits inside the bowel or outside it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what the gas sits inside. The same spot does not mean the same gas.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A perforated ulcer is the most common cause of free gas, so the link feels natural. But most common is a frequency, not a rule.
Check whether the gas is free at all before you name its cause.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read the word 'most': the ulcer is the commonest cause of free gas, not the only one.

say.text: Two checks: is the gas inside the bowel or outside it, and what does the patient look like?
Let me walk one film, step by step. Step 1 is location: gas under the right dome is where free gas usually shows on an erect film.
Step 2 is content. Haustral markings are the colon's own pattern, so this gas lies inside bowel: the Chilaiditi sign, not free gas.
Step 3 is the patient. He is well with a soft belly, so nothing points to gas escaping through a hole.
Now a supine film. Step 1 is done: the gas lies under the right hemidiaphragm.
Step 2 is yours: a bowel loop shows gas on both sides of its wall. Which sign is that?

choices.label: Rigler's sign: both walls of a bowel loop seen
Chilaiditi sign: colon lying under the diaphragm, seen on film
Football sign: a large oval gas shadow over the abdomen
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Rigler's sign is gas on both sides of a bowel wall, which only gas outside the bowel can give.
The step the film hinges on is the finding, not the place where the gas sits.
That choice is not right.
The colon under the diaphragm is tempting, because a gas shadow sits in the same spot. It is the Chilaiditi sign, a pseudo-sign.
Match the finding the stem describes, not the position.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the finding itself: what does the film show about the bowel wall?

say.text: That choice is not right.
A big gas shadow over the abdomen looks like free gas, and the football sign does belong to that family, so the name is easy to grab.
Match the finding in the stem, word for word.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so match the finding word for word, not the overall picture.

say.text: Read the finding in the stem: what does it show about the bowel wall?
A 60-year-old man has a rigid abdomen and free gas on his film. He has never had indigestion, and no one has asked about pain tablets.
What is the right reading?

choices.label: Probably a perforation from an ulcer, so still take the history
Probably an ulcer, since free gas usually comes from one, so theatre
Probably a perforated ulcer, and the history adds little once gas shows
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Free gas with a rigid belly is a perforation, and an ulcer is the likeliest cause, but the history still counts.
Most common tells you the odds, not the certainty for one patient.
That choice is not right.
Free gas usually does come from an ulcer, which is why theatre looks like the obvious move.
But usually describes the odds, and it does not settle the cause in one man.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read 'most common': it ranks the causes; it does not close the question.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Once gas shows, the ulcer story feels complete, so the history seems to add little.
Free gas tells you a hole is likely, not which cause made it. The history still helps.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what free gas proves: a hole, not the cause behind it.

say.text: Ask what 'most common' tells you about a single patient, and what the history could still change.
A patient with a suspected perforation cannot sit up or stand, and he is too unwell to be moved far.
Which film gives the best chance of seeing free gas?

choices.label: Left lateral decubitus film, gas seen beside the liver
Supine film, since it is quick and shows gas anywhere
Right lateral decubitus film, to bring gas to the right
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A left lateral decubitus film is the view for a patient who cannot sit, and the gas it shows lies beside the liver.
Next, why the left side works.
That choice is not right.
A supine film is quick, so it is tempting. But gas rises to the highest point, and a supine film may not show it where it rises.
Ask which part of the belly the gas can reach, given how he lies.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the posture before the film: a patient who cannot sit needs a view chosen for how he lies.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Gas sits on the right of an upright film, so a right-sided view looks right. But the side that is up depends on how he lies, not where gas usually sits.
Think about which way he is lying.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate where gas usually sits from which side of the body is uppermost.

say.text: Ask which side of the abdomen rises highest when he lies on each side.
Same patient, now lying on his left side for the film.
Predict: where does free gas collect, and what outlines it?

choices.label: Between the liver and the right abdominal wall, outlined by liver
Under the left diaphragm, where the stomach bubble hides it
Over the pelvis, where gas drops from the bowel
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. On his left side the right side of the abdomen is uppermost, so the gas rises against the liver and the right wall.
That choice is not right.
The left upper belly is tempting, since the stomach bubble is the familiar sight. But on his left side the stomach is the dependent part, not the highest.
Gas goes to the highest point, so trace which side is up first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the stomach bubble is a standing picture; it does not show where gas goes when he lies down.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Gas does drift down when it is low, so the pelvis looks plausible. But free gas rises to the highest point, and the pelvis is not that.
Ask which part of the abdomen is highest when he lies that way.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the direction: free gas rises to the highest part, not to the lowest.

say.text: Work out which side of him is uppermost when he lies on his left, then which organ sits on that side.
Before the erect film, how long should he sit up?

choices.label: About 10 minutes, long enough for gas to climb
Straight away, since free gas rises at once
About 30 minutes, so the gas has fully settled
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about why there is a wait at all: what does the gas have to do first?
Yes. Gas must climb through the abdomen to reach the diaphragm, and that takes about ten minutes of sitting up.
That choice is not right.
Free gas does rise, so an instant film feels efficient. But rising takes time, and the film has to wait for the gas to climb.
Ask how long the gas needs to reach the diaphragm.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pin the reason: gas needs time to travel up before a film can show it.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A longer wait feels safer, so the bigger figure is tempting. But the wait is set by the time gas needs to climb, not by how long you can spare.
Ask what the wait is meant to allow.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so do not stretch the wait: the point is the climb, not the margin.

say.text: A film taken seconds after he was helped up shows no free gas, but his peritonism is plain.
Which step raises the yield?

choices.label: Repeat the film after he has sat up long enough
Repeat the film at once, with him standing
Repeat the film after two hours of bed rest
Take a supine film instead, to be quicker

say.text: Yes. Gas needs the upright time to reach the diaphragm, so the repeat film can show what the first one missed.
That choice is not right.
Standing sounds like a quick way to bring gas up, so the repeat feels sensible. But the film still has to wait for the gas to climb.
Ask what the first film missed, and why.
That choice is not right.
Two hours of rest feels thorough, but the gas does not need a long rest; it needs the upright time to rise.
Ask what the repeat film needs the patient to do.
That choice is not right.
A supine film is quicker, so it is tempting. But the view for a patient who cannot sit is a lateral one, which lets the gas show.
Ask which view his position allows.
